q: Why might one drone carry cameras and sensors while another carries a spray tank?
options: All drones are built identically
Different parts let drones specialize in different tasks, like data collection versus applying inputs
Spray tanks are only decorative
Cameras and spray tanks always come on the same drone
explain: Drones are built with different parts depending on their purpose — sensing drones carry cameras and sensors, while application drones carry tanks for pesticides or fertilizers.

q: What is a key advantage rovers have over drones for scouting?
options: Rovers can fly higher than drones
Rover cameras sit at plant canopy level, giving a different vantage point than aerial imagery
Rovers never need batteries
Rovers are always faster than drones
explain: Rover cameras are positioned at plant canopy level, letting them capture detail that's hard to get from above, such as individual plant or leaf health.

q: How does an AI model identify a pest it has never specifically seen in training?
options: It cannot identify anything new
It randomly guesses
It compares the new image's characteristics against patterns learned from thousands of labeled examples
It requires a human to manually identify every single image
explain: AI models learn overlapping patterns from many labeled examples, then apply that learned pattern recognition to classify new, previously unseen images.

q: Why are sensors especially valuable for agricultural data collection?
options: They can collect data around the clock, including in conditions or times humans cannot easily monitor
They can only work during the day
They replace the need for any human decision-making
They are always cheaper than any other tool
explain: Sensors can be deployed continuously, allowing data collection 24/7 in places and times that would be difficult or impossible for a human to monitor directly.

q: In the Solution Innovator Challenge, why does combined accuracy multiply across tools instead of averaging?
options: Multiplying makes the math simpler
Averaging isn't a real math operation
Because each tool in the workflow introduces its own chance of error, and those probabilities compound together
The workbook specifies accuracy must always equal 100%
explain: Each step in a workflow — sensing, identification, management — carries its own accuracy. Multiplying those probabilities together reflects how errors can compound across multiple steps, rather than canceling out through averaging.

q: Why must a workflow address both insect and weed management separately, even if using a tool that supports both?
options: Insects and weeds are the same type of pest
Because different tools have different scopes — some only manage weeds, some only manage insects, and some can handle both
Only insects ever need management
Weeds never require any active management
explain: Tools like One Pass Cultivation only address weeds, while Biological Control only addresses insects. Tools like the Tractor Sprayer and Sprayer Drone can handle both, but a workflow still needs to confirm coverage of each pest type.
